description: Select source with COPY and keep filename entry out of the new assembler.
why: The bootstrap ladder already has an assembler. We can retain its tested parser and use fixed files for the next tool.

Copy the completed ASM86 source. OPENFILE uses SOURCE.ASM, and the final writer uses RESULT.COM. The driver no longer calls GETNAME. The instruction language and the old whole-image buffer are otherwise unchanged at this stopping point.

The two input passes still finish before output creation. Keep ASMKEEP.COM as the preceding assembler; its existing filename prompt builds each native checkpoint. COPY selects the source for the new tool.

title: Reading an input block
description: Refill a small block instead of making a DOS call for every byte.
why: A sequential reader can handle a long file with bounded working storage.
explain:
NEXTBYTE retains its interface: AX is one with CHAR set, or zero at EOF. RDPOS and RDLEN describe bytes already returned by DOS. A refill requests 1024 bytes at 5000H. Any positive returned count is consumed completely before another refill; a short positive read is not EOF.

The driver clears both fields at the start of each pass. NEXTBYTE changes AX, BX, CX, DX, flags, CHAR, and the two cursors, while preserving SI, DI, and BP. The line and token readers therefore need no new calling convention.

title: Writing an output block
description: Copy a stream through a bounded output block and inspect the result.
why: The emitter needs a working file writer before it can replace the assembler image buffer.
explain:
This checkpoint is a byte-copy diagnostic. The parser remains in the source but the driver does not call it. CREATEOUT opens ASMA.TMP, EMIT stores one byte into the 1024-byte output block, and FLUSH writes a full or final partial block. PC counts bytes from the chosen 0100H origin and refuses an image beyond EFFFH.

FLUSH preserves AX, BX, CX, and DX. It checks DOS carry and the actual written count; zero buffered bytes cause no DOS write. CLOSEOUT checks the final close. This diagnostic may overwrite ASMA.TMP and leaves that file after success. Its contents are data, not a program to execute.

title: Cleaning an interrupted output
description: Track handles and temporary-file ownership separately.
why: A failed assembly must not leave its own partial temporary output looking usable.
explain:
ERROR saves its category before CLEANUP can change AX. INOPEN and OUTOPEN describe live handles; OWNTMP says whether this run created ASMA.TMP. Cleanup closes the owned handles and removes its own temporary file. It never deletes RESULT.COM.

A failed close or delete sets CLEANFAIL. The error report includes a recovery notice when files may need inspection. Cleanup does not recurse into ERROR. The copy driver still leaves ASMA.TMP after success, but a failed input open now removes its newly created empty temporary file.

title: Protecting recovery names
description: Refuse an occupied temporary or backup name before creating output.
why: An earlier interrupted run may have left a file worth recovering.
explain:
EXISTS opens an ordinary fixed disk name read-only, closes it if found, and returns one; only file-not-found returns zero. Other DOS failures remain errors. PREFLIGHT checks ASMA.TMP and RESULT.BAK and reports category eight if either is present.

The checks occur before CREATEOUT. A reserved file is not silently erased. Inspect or rename a leftover file before trying again. AX, BX, and DOS flags are scratch during existence checks.

title: Publishing a closed result
description: Rename a completed temporary file into its public name.
why: A result should be replaced only after all its bytes and its close have succeeded.
explain:
COMMIT moves an older RESULT.COM to RESULT.BAK, renames ASMA.TMP to RESULT.COM, then removes the backup. HAVEBAK and OWNTMP record the state of that sequence. If publication fails after the backup move, restoration is attempted; failed restoration retains both recovery files.

A failed backup removal also prevents OK. DOS rename is not atomic replacement, so the recovery names are explicit. The driver here still copies test data. RESULT.COM from this checkpoint is inspected with VIEW.BAS and must not be executed.

title: Streaming the two assembly passes
description: Return to the assembler with no complete image buffer.
why: The tested block writer can now receive bytes as pass two produces them.
explain:
Pass one records definitions and counts instruction bytes without writing. Its final PC is saved in ENDPC. Pass two creates the temporary output, reopens the source, emits incrementally, and must finish at the same PC. FLUSH, CLOSEOUT, and COMMIT run only after successful source close.

PC describes the target; OUTCNT describes the current block. They are independent. Input, parser, or range errors remove this run's temporary file and preserve an older RESULT.COM. The accepted language remains the published ASM86 vocabulary.

why: A source file can contain much more text than its executable contains bytes.

description: Teach an instruction form before using it in a successor.

The seed implementation still uses only instructions accepted by ASM86. It encodes these forms as output for another program; it does not yet execute them. Register widths and mixed segment/ordinary forms are checked explicitly.

title: Proving the seed handoff
description: Build ASMA0 with ASM86 and compare two self-assembly generations.
why: A successor becomes a rung of the ladder only when its preceding builder can make it.
explain:
The source is the preceding tested checkpoint, saved here under a permanent seed name. ASM86 builds it directly. ASMA0 then reads that same source through SOURCE.ASM, writes RESULT.COM, and must reproduce its own executable. A second generation must match too.

Keep the initial ASM86-built executable while making both comparisons. The seed has streaming I/O, 2048 symbols, a larger output profile, and explicit segment access. No outside assembler supplies an executable.

title: Allocating auxiliary workspace
description: Shrink the main allocation and request owned DOS work blocks.
why: A full symbol table should not compete with resident code for the same segment.
explain:
MEMINIT checks the owned main segment, retains 1000H paragraphs with DOS function 4AH, allocates eight A00H-paragraph pages and one 200H-paragraph bucket block, and clears every bucket head. Returned segments are saved in MEMSEGS; HASHSEG follows the eight page words.

MEMFREE releases recorded allocations and restores ES to the main segment. Partial-allocation failure uses the same cleanup. The assembler still uses its seed symbol table in this checkpoint; normal checked assembly confirms the auxiliary setup completed.

title: Selecting a symbol page
description: Translate a stable symbol ID into a page and offset.
why: A page selector and offset must travel together inside a table helper.
explain:
SYMPTR takes an ID from one through 8192 in AX. Subtracting one yields a page number in groups of 1024 and an index within that page. Forty times the index is the record offset in BX; ES selects its allocated page. RECORDPTR saves that offset.

The entry diagnostic selects ID 8192, writes and reads word 42, restores ES, and compares the loaded word with 42 and rejects a mismatch. It uses the final record slot in the final page. Ordinary assembler processing still uses the retained seed table; the test does not make an arbitrary offset into a main-segment pointer.

title: Looking up the complete spelling
description: Use buckets to find candidates and compare every character.
why: A hash narrows a search but cannot decide whether two names are equal.
explain:
SYMLOOK folds the name into a sixteen-bit rotating hash, selects one of 4096 word buckets, then follows record IDs. Every candidate is compared with the complete spelling through its zero terminator. HEADID retains the original bucket head while SYMID follows the chain.

The entry test looks up PAGED before insertion, writes its record into the selected bucket, then looks it up again and compares the saved value with 12345 and rejects a mismatch. It restores the line cursor and ES. Colliding names remain distinct; no name is accepted merely because its hash matches.

title: Using the paged symbol table
description: Move definition and value resolution onto the new record helpers.
why: The table is ready to replace the seed's fixed in-segment records.
explain:
DEFINE validates a name and register exclusion, refuses duplicates, and creates at most 8192 records. Pass two requires the stored value and kind to agree and marks each definition seen once. DEFSEEN must equal SYMC at the end, in addition to the final PC check.

SYMBOLVALUE finds a record and returns its word value. An unresolved pass-one reference returns a placeholder and sets UNRESOLVED; pass two rejects it. The line/token and I/O addresses still use the seed layout here, so the new table can be checked independently of another buffer move.

description: Move parser and file buffers above a generous resident-image area.
why: A larger assembler needs a memory map which permits its own code and source vocabulary to grow.

The main segment reserves 0100H through BFFFH for code and static data, C800H through CBFFH for the line, CC00H through CC3FH for a token, and separate 4 KB I/O blocks at D000H and E000H. The stack reservation remains F000H through FFFFH.

Names may contain thirty-one characters; tokens may contain sixty-three; a physical line may contain 1023 characters. The 8192 forty-byte symbol records live outside the main segment. Both the scanner and symbol validator check their own bounds before copying.

description: Report source positions with a checked pair of words.
why: A source file with many comments and definitions can exceed a sixteen-bit line count.

COUNTLINE and COUNTINPUT maintain low/high word pairs and refuse a full-pair wrap. The driver clears the pairs for each pass. NUMBER32 prints ten decimal digits using paired subtraction; ERROR now displays the complete line number.

The byte count records consumed source bytes; a positive short refill is still consumed before reading again. Source counters do not resize an image buffer. A small BASIC text exercise can create a long comment source without requiring a person to type repeated lines.

title: Quoted byte data
description: Preserve string bytes while folding names outside quotes.
why: Readable messages should not require entering every character as a numeric byte.
explain:
READLINE retains the original character case. SCAN folds identifier characters and treats quote as a delimiter. DATAITEM reads quoted DB content directly from the physical line, so it is not limited to the ordinary token length. A doubled quote emits one quote; a semicolon inside a string is data.

Strings can be mixed with numeric DB items. DW rejects quoted strings. A string cannot cross a physical line and must close before its terminator. The test deliberately includes lowercase and a semicolon.

title: Small value expressions
description: Evaluate unary signs, grouping, addition, subtraction, and the current address.
why: Addresses and counts often differ from a named value by a small offset.
explain:
VALUE combines FACTOR results left to right. FACTOR recognizes a number or symbol through ATOM, unary plus/minus, parentheses, and $. Native stack saves keep intermediate values distinct during recursive parsing. EXPRDEPTH bounds active factors at sixteen.

Values wrap as words, but byte and size contexts still check their own ranges. UNRESOLVED propagates through a first-pass expression so a provisional value cannot silently decide a layout count. The test uses only arithmetic whose byte results are known.

title: Named assembly constants
description: Give a known value a name without allocating bytes.
why: An explicit constant can replace repeated counts while leaving the location counter unchanged.
explain:
STATEMENT saves the first spelling before looking for EQU. Its expression must be resolved on pass one, then RESTORENAME restores the definition token for DEFINE. DEFTYPE distinguishes this absolute constant from a loaded label.

Forward or cyclic EQU definitions are rejected. Earlier labels and constants may participate in an expression, including a difference from $. Pass two must reproduce the same constant and kind. Defining a constant emits no bytes.

RESERVE evaluates a resolved count and rejects an unresolved layout value. RESW checks before doubling the count; both forms check against the remaining image space before emitting any zeroes. EMIT then streams the zero-filled region through the same output block.

The reserved bytes exist in the flat COM file. They are not a request for extra DOS memory. An image may fill offsets 0100H through EFFFH, with F000H as its end label, while the assembler's own workspace remains separate.

title: One ModR/M emitter
description: Encode register or memory fields through one checked path.
why: Address-byte construction should be shared by the instructions that use it.
explain:
ENCODE emits an optional segment prefix, the chosen opcode, and the ModR/M byte. RMMOD selects no displacement, a byte displacement, or a word displacement; direct mode zero with code six also emits a word address. Register mode adds 192.

CHECKWIDTH infers an unspecified memory width from a register and rejects an explicit disagreement. The MOV bridges provide their opcode and register field, then use the common emitter. Known-width and immediate helpers are separate entry points for instructions needing those rules.

description: Parse valid base/index combinations and explicit displacements.
why: A word within a record, array, or procedure frame needs more than one fixed address form.

A written displacement always uses its word form, even when zero or temporarily unresolved. The complete test establishes a BP frame, reads its argument at BP+4, stores a local at BP-2, and releases that local before returning.

title: Proving the larger assembler
description: Compare the seed-built program with two native self-assembly generations.
why: The expanded assembler is another working rung, not a source listing dependent on an outside tool.
explain:
Save the preceding source as ASM86A.ASM. ASMA0 builds its first executable from that source. ASM86A then assembles the same source twice and both outputs must match the seed-built original. Keep each known working generation under a distinct short disk name.

The tool uses fixed files, streamed I/O, 8192 exact-spelling symbols, an allocated workspace, and the documented native language. The complete ladder exercise carries its output into the IR86 and RILL tools.
